name: Bukola Arikawe
missingPieces: D1 missing the hardcoded JWT secret finding (sankofa-legacy-admin-2019). Decoy misidentified in both D1 and D3 (alg:none chosen instead of the safe hash_equals HS256 branch). D2 CVSS vectors carry wrong A:H/S:C metrics. D4 cites NDPA Part 1 but no section number.
feedback: D1 is a solid catalogue. You caught SQL injection with both the concatenated query at lines 47-48 and the admin' OR '1'='1 capture at 02:15:31, the alg:none acceptance with Token 2, the missing token expiry, the insecure cookie, stored XSS with the beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443, open redirect, path traversal and XXE, almost all with a quoted line or timestamp. Two things cost you. You never found the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 around lines 30 and 38, which is one of the ten and a clean A05/CWE-798. More seriously you misidentified the decoy: the safe construct in this pack is the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant-time and sound, and you were meant to name it and prove it safe. You instead pointed at alg:none and called it exploitable, which is correct as a finding but wrong as the decoy answer, so that row scores zero. Your MD5 finding is right on the mechanism but you filed it under A03 Injection when it is A02 Cryptographic Failures. D2 reconstructs the chain well with verbatim payloads for SQLi, the alg:none token, the XSS beacon, the file read and the full XXE document, and you tie steps to 02:15:31, 02:18:47 and 02:24:02. You dropped the open redirect hop at 02:21:13 and the recon and failed-guess lines, so the chain is shorter than the evidence supports. Your CVSS vectors are complete strings, which is good, but several metrics are wrong: SQLi should be A:N not A:H so it is about 9.1, not 9.8, because the login bypass does not touch availability, and your A:H justification of potential service disruption does not hold for read-and-bypass bugs. The strongest scope insight, that a forged super_admin token reaches the shared /api/v1/internal service for a real S:C, is the kind of reasoning your S:C cells needed and you asserted scope change without it. Your impact of 300 to 400 million naira is high: 312 accounts capped near 950,000 each, with most far lower, lands in the tens of millions, so state the averaging assumption rather than extrapolating to the top of the range. D3 reads cleanly, the executive summary ends on 312 customers and a naira headline, findings are tied to evidence, and crucially your remediation table is ordered by effort with hours and days and an explicit earliest-break statement that fixing SQL injection first buys the most risk reduction for the least work, which is exactly what we wanted. Your two detection stopgaps name concrete fields and false-positive rates. What is thin is the threat model, which is barely present, and you repeat the decoy error by treating alg:none as the disproved construct instead of disproving the hash_equals branch. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice and anchors to 05-exfil-sample.csv and the 02:15:31 timestamp, and you cite ISC2 Canon I and II by number. It falls short on the NDPA: you reference Part 1 but not the load-bearing sections, which are section 40 for the 72-hour notification to the NDPC and section 41 for notifying the 312 data subjects on high risk, and naming those by number is what the prompt asked. Nothing here is fabricated, your figures trace to the sample even where the range is too high. I looked for a way to push this into the mid-70s and the missing tenth finding, the misidentified decoy across two deliverables, and the wrong CVSS metrics did not support it. The single most important fix is to identify the real decoy correctly: name the hash_equals HS256 branch and prove at the mechanism level that constant-time comparison makes it safe, rather than flagging alg:none, which is a genuine vulnerability.
